title: A Systematic Comparison of Contextualized Word Embeddings for Lexical Semantic Change

selection.evidence: Cited by saponara2026 ([17]) as the source for XL-LEXEME being the state of the art for LSCD; read to know what numbers an XL-LEXEME pipeline reaches on the DWUG-family benchmarks that arena-lsc uses as its public dev pool.

cost.compute_notes: Main body pp. 1-9 read in full (PyMuPDF text; tables parsed from text, column order checked against headers); appendices (pp. 10-21: per-layer results, benchmark statistics) skimmed for table captions only. No artifact run here; code at github.com/FrancescoPeriti/CSSDetection not cloned.

triggers: which contextual embedding model is best for semantic change detection
APD vs PRT vs cluster JSD graded change detection
XL-LEXEME vs GPT-4 word in context
does clustering help semantic change detection
WSI evaluation on DWUG with ARI and purity

claims.statement: Under equal settings on 8 LSC benchmarks (EN LA DE SV ES RU NO ZH), XL-LEXEME is the best embedding for graded change detection with every approach; APD > PRT > WiDiD > AP+JSD. Weighted-average Spearman with XL-LEXEME: APD .751, PRT .693, WiDiD .422, AP+JSD .223.
claims.scope: Embeddings of the annotated usages only (not full corpora), last layer, no fine-tuning beyond XL-LEXEME's own; AP = affinity propagation; weighted by number of targets.

our_assessment.why: Numbers are read from Table 1 as printed (not recomputed). The form-vs-sense gap is large and consistent across benchmarks, but 'sense-based' here means AP/APP clustering; the paper itself shows (Section 5.4) that clustering with the benchmark's own correlation-clustering pipeline on XL-LEXEME similarities gives GCD .754 - so the weakness is AP, not 'clusters' as such. For SemEval-2027 Task 3, whose 1b is computed only from a clustering, that distinction is the whole game.

claims.statement: As computational annotators of usage pairs (cosine as a proximity judgment), XL-LEXEME correlates with human judgments at about human-human agreement (EN Spearman .626 vs Krippendorff alpha .633; GPT-4 .606); pre-trained BERT/mBERT/XLM-R are far lower (avg .358/.301/.272).
claims.scope: Only pairs that humans judged; WiC graded framework; GPT-4 on EN only.

our_assessment.why: Spearman with mean judgments vs Krippendorff's alpha among annotators are different statistics, so 'close to human level' is an analogy, not a comparison on one scale. Still the practical point holds: on pairs, XL-LEXEME is as good as the best LLM tested, at a fraction of the cost.

claims.statement: WSI by correlation clustering of the XL-LEXEME-annotated usage graph reaches ARI about .27-.45 and purity .77-.84 against the human DWUG clusters; GCD from those clusters averages .754.
claims.scope: Same clustering algorithm as used to build the gold, applied to the model's similarities on judged pairs only.

our_assessment.why: Partly circular by design (same clustering as the gold, and only the gold's sampled edges), which the authors acknowledge. It bounds what a 'model replaces the annotators' pipeline gets on DWUG; it does not say what a full all-pairs clustering gets.

checked.how: link read in the PDF footnote; not cloned

relations.why: Same authors, same year; the position paper argues for the sense-based modelling this paper finds weak.

open_questions: How does all-pairs correlation clustering (the WUG algorithm) on XL-LEXEME similarities compare with average-linkage agglomerative clustering for SemEval-2027 Task 3 1a/1b? Testable on the arena-lsc public pool.
